preserved_objections.basis: The asymmetric octant segments would create flow dead zones where biofilm accumulation would be worse than in standard designs, directly contradicting the claimed benefit of disrupting biofilm formation.

The candidate claims effectiveness in non-chlorinated water environments (<0.5 ppm), but the evidence shows stainless steel stress corrosion cracking occurs even in low-chloride environments, making the proposed design vulnerable in real-world district cooling systems.

The cited evidence (doi:10.3323/jcorr1974.29.7_354) demonstrates stainless steel heat exchangers fail due to chloride-induced corrosion, yet the candidate proposes using stainless steel with modified geometry without addressing this fundamental material limitation.

The claimed heat transfer coefficient of 2500 W/m2K is not substantiated by any evidence in the bundle, and the pressure drop prediction of <15% increase over 12 months is unsubstantiated given the known failure modes in similar systems.

Manufacturing asymmetric octant segments with the required precision for a plate heat exchanger would be prohibitively expensive and would compromise the structural integrity of the plates under thermal cycling conditions.

The candidate fails to specify how the "multidirectional flow patterns" would be measured or verified, making the core mechanism untestable and the prediction of maintained heat transfer coefficient impossible to validate.
